## 1. Word order and the notion of symmetry

The classical Latin construction, with its multiple possibilities, must have surprised you, and perhaps it even seemed to you to stem from the purest fancy.

In fact, the order of words in the simple clause seems as if it could be anything at all. Thus the elementary sentence Euclio Congrionem verberat (*Euclio is beating Congrio*) can theoretically be said in six different ways (E.C.V.; E.V.C.; V.E.C.; V.C.E.; C.E.V.; C.V.E.). These six forms are all grammatically correct, but they are not identical as to sense: each one makes it possible to express a particular nuance.

The most banal order is the order: SUBJECT, COMPLEMENT (direct), VERB: the sentence E.C.V. is therefore the only one that contains no additional nuance. Any modification of this order will bring one: thus, if one wants to insist on the fact that it is Congrio who receives the blows, one can put Congrio first and say: Congrionem Euclio verberat.

Likewise if one wants to insist on the fact that it is a matter of giving blows, one will put the verb at the head (V.E.C. or V.C.E.), according to the respective (secondary) importance of E. and of C. But let us not give too much importance to the sense of the different possible combinations, for there as elsewhere PRACTICE often differs from THEORY. So do not go too far in this direction and wait to be well informed by USAGE: it is the best of all guides.

What is true for the order of words in the simple clause is often true for the order of clauses in the complex sentence. Thus, in is fecit cui prodest (w. f. w. *that one [it] has done to whom it profits* = *the one who did it is the one to whom it profits*), these two clauses can be inverted: cui prodest is fecit (*it is the one to whom it profits who did it*). You should not have any difficulty grasping the nuance that distinguishes these two sentences.

When the number of words and the number of clauses increases, one may think that the situation quickly becomes inextricable. Now the Romans found their way about in it very well: why not us? Before making fuller acquaintance with this plank of salvation that is the «NOTION OF SYMMETRY», let us first see what must not be done.

The most frequent error consists in hooking onto nouns epithets, appositions or predicates which do not relate to them. If, in French, the epithet is almost always found next to the noun to which it relates, it is quite otherwise in Latin. Examples:

### a) Porcellum imitans, adultus porcellus videberis

(L. 79, P. 11): Porcellum (accusative) cannot be the subject and imitans cannot be its apposition. But the fact that the verb (videberis) is in the 2nd person lights everything up:

- imitans (nominative),<sup>1</sup> apposition to the understood subject; Porcellum, direct object complement of the present participle imitans (order cpt-verb); and the whole Porcellum imitans is the equivalent of a conditional clause: *if you imitate P.*
- adultus (nominative) can likewise only relate to the understood subject (tu). This word is a perfect participle (at once verb and adjective): it can be considered as a temporal clause (cf. grammatical appendix) equivalent to cum adultus factus eris, *when you have become adult*.
- Finally porcellus videberis is quite simply a main clause: subject tu, understood; verb videberis; and porcellus (nominative), predicate of the subject, this function being confirmed by the order of the words, for the predicate, like the direct object complement, is placed preferably just before the verb: *you will look like a little pig*.

But, you will say, and quite rightly, this analysis of the sentence is not LIVING. And how does one do it to understand a conversation? If you have listened to the records, you may have noticed that all this could be learnt intuitively. If not here is an explanation which will be useful to you:

The only difficulty of Latin word order is that it makes greater use<sup>2</sup> of the possibilities of memory: it is enough to take this into account. When I listen to a sentence, I put the words on hold in my memory by instinctively sticking labels on them; thus, in our example:

- Porcellum, accusative, is therefore going to undergo something;
- imitans, present participle, it's a verb; so there is already indicated the action that the preceding Porcellum undergoes. But it is at the same time an adjective, probably in the nominative (what follows will tell us); therefore which relates to the subject I am calmly waiting for;
- adultus, perfect participle (if I take it as an adjective, that changes nothing in comprehension), in the nominative; therefore relates to the subject and confirms the supposition put forward (imitans = nominative) for the preceding; before and after adultus, the voice marks a slight pause; therefore adultus is not an epithet but is equivalent to an adverbial clause (see above);
- porcellus, in the nominative: either subject, or epithet, apposition or predicate of the subject, this last hypothesis being confirmed as soon as there appears
- videberis which, after having definitively settled the relations between the preceding words, puts the full stop.

These operations thus described seem to you even longer than those of the previous analysis: in fact they are much briefer, for usage makes them instinctive, therefore almost instantaneous. Besides if you wanted to describe the way in which the elements of a French sentence that you understand intuitively are treated in turn in your brain, you would notice that the operation is just as complicated.

### b) In aedibus quid tibi meis erat negotii

Another example (L. 83, P. 1): in aedibus quid tibi meis erat negotii. Meis can only relate to aedibus for, in the sentence, only these two words are in the ablative<sup>3</sup> plural; negotii cannot be a nominative plural for there is no verb in the plural: it is therefore a genitive singular, therefore the complement of a noun or of a pronoun,<sup>4</sup> in this case of the pronoun quid.

But this analysis is still tedious! You can arrive effortlessly at the same result if you want to take account of the fact that this sentence is constructed with a certain SYMMETRY:

Aedibus is symmetrical with its epithet meis relative to the group quid tibi; likewise quid is symmetrical with negotii relative to tibi… erat: the diagram below will help you grasp the spirit of the construction:

```
In aedibus .............. meis    at my place
      quid ........ negotii       what (of) occupation
         tibi ... erat            to you was
```

## 2. The beacons of the complex sentence

IN THE COMPLEX SENTENCE, one will find an analogous structure: nesting of words and sometimes of clauses, arranged in such a way as to make the sentence more compact. Fortunately there exist signposts that clearly show the path to follow amid this apparent complexity: these are the CORRELATIVE WORDS. There are several sorts of them:

**a) Demonstratives and relatives.** — Example: is… qui:

- is fecit cui prodest, *that one (it) has done to whom (it) profits*; or, by inverting the two clauses:
- cui prodest, is fecit, *it is the one to whom it profits who did it* (note the economy of words that the flexibility of Latin permits).

Likewise talis (*such*)… qualis (*what*), such: qualis pater, talis filius, *like father, like son*.

**b) Correlative adverbs of place.** — Example: ibi (*here*)… ubi (*where*):

- si ibi adfuisses ubi tibi erat negotium, *if you had been there (ibi) where (ubi) you had business*.

Likewise for the question quo?: eo… quo: si eo adisses quo tibi eundum erat, *if you had gone there where you had to go*.

And finally inde… unde and ea… qua for the questions unde? and qua?

As we indicated to you above, the order of the clauses can be inverted: si ubi tibi erat negotium ibi adfuisses, or even profoundly modified. Thus (in L. 83, P. 10) Plautus grouped the words ibi ubi tibi to obtain a comic effect.

**c) Correlative adverbs of time.** — Example: cum (*as, when*)… tum (*then*):

- cum hirundines demisse volant tum imber imminens est, *when swallows fly low [then] the rain is (threatening) [near]*.

**d) Correlative adverbs and adjectives of quantity.** — Example: tantus, -a, -um (*so great*)… quantus, -a, -um (*as great*):

- tantum aquae habebam quantum ad potum satis esset (L. 72, P. 4).

ATTENTION! the adjectives being declinable, you can find the two terms in different genders, numbers and cases.

**e) Other correlative words.** — You have already met in pairs a certain number of conjunctions: adeo… ut, *to such a point that*; ita… ut, *in such a way that*; sic… ut, *in the same way as*; sicut… sic, *in the same way as… in the same way*, etc.

Finally a pair of correlative words can be composed of two terms of different kinds. Example tantus, -a, -um… ut, *big enough… for*.

It is useless to go further for the moment. Simply remember that Latin makes great use of these correlative words. Each time you know how to recognize them, you will better grasp the sense of the sentence. Do not forget that the order of the correlative words can be inverted (sic… ut or ut… sic), that they can be united (sicut) or on the contrary separated by several clauses or even several sentences, and finally that the demonstrative term can be understood (fecit cui prodest).

If you want to know more about it, you will find the most important of these words, classed by categories, in the grammatical appendix. But above all, make their acquaintance by reading and rereading many Latin sentences and trying to forget their French translation. Thanks to practice, you will notice that everything that still seems artificial to you will soon become natural.

## 3. Prefixes (continued)

Let us look again at a few prefixes which are also prepositions:

| Prefix | Idea | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| ex | a) going out | exire, *to go out*; expetere (L. 83, P. 6), *to claim* |
| | b) completion | exhaurire, *to draw completely, to exhaust* |
| in | in, on | ingredi, *to enter into* |
| per | a) through | percurrere, *to run through* |
| | b) completely | perficere, *to complete, to perfect* |
| trans | beyond | transmittere, *to transmit*; tranare, *to cross by swimming* |

This revision is long, but we hope that it will have interested you. We preferred to wait for the end of the work to explain to you the very important question of word order. Indeed, for the first wave instinctive assimilation took precedence over everything.

Do not forget that this first study must be followed by a second wave… and even by a third if you feel the need. That will be the occasion for you to put your new knowledge to good use.

Now, to progress, it will be good to seek to understand.

Today, you must revise lesson 35.

---

1. Imitans could be a neuter accusative, but this hypothesis is easily eliminated.
2. And, if it is well used, it allows a better yield in the transmission of information: see above the very simple example of is fecit cui prodest and compare its concision with the length of its translations. This quality, if it is well used, is even more precious when one must express very complex ideas.
3. Or in the dative, a hypothesis that is easily eliminated.
4. The hypotheses: complement in the genitive of a verb such as memini, or locative are to be eliminated.
